title: Fairness-Constrained Training Benchmark
one_liner: A standard test suite shows which algorithms actually train fair neural networks and which ones fail, using real census data with actual equity problems.
lead: Training a neural network to be fair — to avoid approving loans more often for some groups than others — is hard. No standard way exists to test whether an algorithm really works. This paper builds a real-world benchmark using census income data, where you can measure if an algorithm genuinely improves fairness without just cutting accuracy to pieces, because the benchmark locks all variables except the loss formula itself, so any difference between algorithms is real, not due to lucky hyperparameters or different testing conditions.

problem.h2: The fairness-training problem has no referee
paras: When you build a machine-learning model to predict income from census data, it often turns out biased. It might approve loans at 90% for one group but only 60% for another. A naive fix is to add a fairness penalty to the training loss — a small term that punishes unfair predictions. But which penalty formula works best? How much should you penalize? Nobody really knows, because there's no standard test ground to compare them fairly.

If you try one algorithm and it seems to work, you don't know if it's actually good or just lucky on your particular data. If you compare three algorithms by running each one once, you might pick the wrong winner because of random noise in training. And most algorithms have never been implemented at all, so they sit in papers untested in practice.

callout.html: The paper builds a standard fairness-training benchmark so you can actually measure which algorithms work and which fail.

steps.text: US Census income records with demographics: age, gender, race, education, income yes/no.
Specify a fairness rule: e.g. approval rates must be within 5% for all demographic groups.
Each uses a different formula to add fairness pressure during training; train each to convergence.
On held-out test data: what fraction of each group gets approved fairly, and what overall accuracy?

steps.b: Compare directly on the same ground
steps.text: See which algorithm achieves the best fairness-accuracy tradeoff, without random noise clouding the picture.

paras: The paper does not change the neural network itself. Instead, it changes the loss function — the scoreboard that tells training which direction to nudge weights. Normally the loss only measures accuracy error. The paper compares three different ways to add a fairness penalty to that scoreboard, so training pulls in two directions at once: toward correct predictions and toward fair ones.
object.object: training loss formula with fairness penalty

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: the fairness-accuracy frontier
hidden.name: fairness-accuracy tradeoff curve
paras: When you train to be fair, you usually have to give up some accuracy. Train harder for fairness, accuracy drops. Train purely for accuracy, fairness tanks. The paper measures this tradeoff — how much accuracy does each fairness level cost — and plots it as a curve for each algorithm. That curve is the hidden quantity that matters: it shows whether an algorithm is efficient (gets more fairness for less accuracy loss) or wasteful (burns accuracy without gaining fairness).

The paper estimates this by running each algorithm multiple times with different fairness-penalty strengths (weak penalty, medium, strong) and plotting the results. The algorithm whose curve sits highest and rightmost — high fairness, high accuracy — is the winner.

heat.caption: Darker means more fairness pressure. Highlighted cells change as penalty strength increases.

reads.html: The fairness-accuracy tradeoff is a curve showing: if you force fairness to X level, you sacrifice accuracy down to Y level. Different algorithms have different curves — some are steep (wasteful), some are flat (efficient).

The paper measures the Pareto frontier of the constrained optimization problem: for each algorithm and each feasible fairness constraint, what is the maximum achievable accuracy? That frontier is the hidden quantity being benchmarked.

mechanism.h2: Why the benchmark reveals the truth
paras: The core reason this benchmark works is that it removes all the noise and excuses. Each algorithm runs on the same data, with the same fairness rule, on the same neural network architecture. The only thing that differs is the loss formula. So if one algorithm wins, it's not because someone got lucky or picked a better learning rate — it's because the algorithm itself is smarter about balancing fairness and accuracy.

The benchmark also tests at scale: real census data with thousands of examples and real demographic imbalance (some groups are smaller, some more common). This catches algorithms that work in toy examples but crumble on realistic messy data. An algorithm might seem fair on a toy 100-row dataset but fail when you scale to 100,000 rows with class imbalance and overlapping demographics.

stages.s: Run Algorithm A with fairness penalty
Measure fairness gap and accuracy on test set
Repeat for Algorithm B and C
Plot all three curves side by side
Clear winner: which algorithm has best fairness-accuracy tradeoff

math.words: total loss equals accuracy error plus lambda times fairness penalty, where lambda controls how much to prioritize fairness
symbols: the total loss (error score training tries to minimize)
the fairness weight: higher means prioritize fairness more, ignore some accuracy loss
a measure of unfairness: often the gap in approval rates between groups
the difference in how often each demographic group gets approved

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say Group A approval rate is 80%, Group B is 60%. Fairness gap = 20 percentage points.
Accuracy loss: 15 wrong predictions out of 100 total = 0.15.
Fairness penalty: gap_squared = 20^2 = 400. With lambda=0.01, fairness loss = 0.01 * 400 = 4.0.
Total loss = 0.15 + 4.0 = 4.15. Training tries to lower this. It can shrink accuracy loss by better predicting, OR shrink fairness loss by narrowing the approval gap (bringing both groups to ~70%).

If lambda=0.1 instead, fairness loss becomes 0.1 * 400 = 40.0, total = 40.15. Now fairness pressure is 10x stronger, so training works harder to close the gap, even if it means slightly worse accuracy.

math.note: Training picks the path that lowers total loss fastest: nudge the group approval rates toward equal, while also getting predictions right.

charts.title: Algorithm 1: Naive fairness penalty
rows: Fairness gap: points of difference in approval rates
charts.note: Closes fairness gap but at high accuracy cost; efficiency is poor, because the naive loss formula does not adapt its penalty strength as training progresses.

charts.title: Algorithm 2: Lagrange multiplier method
rows: Fairness gap: points of difference in approval rates
charts.note: Balances both objectives well; lets the algorithm adjust penalty strength dynamically, because it treats fairness as a constraint and tunes the multiplier to find the best feasible point.

charts.title: Algorithm 3: Per-group reweighting
rows: Fairness gap: points of difference in approval rates
charts.note: Achieves tightest fairness but sacrifices too much accuracy; the curve is steep, because this method reweights training samples without a tuning knob to dial in the right tradeoff.

items.b: Data leakage: sensitive attributes slip into features
items.html: If the training data contains age or gender numbers by accident, the model can achieve fairness by luck, not by learning to be fair. The benchmark must carefully remove sensitive attributes from the input but still measure fairness on them at test time.

If the algorithm optimizes for demographic parity (equal approval rates) but the test measures equalized odds (equal error rates), the algorithm might win on one metric but lose on another. The benchmark must be clear about which fairness definition it uses.

If you tune learning rate and batch size to help Algorithm A but not Algorithm B, A will look better unfairly, because a faster learning rate trains harder toward the goal (fairness or accuracy) that Algorithm A focuses on. The benchmark must use identical hyperparameters for all three or tune fairly.
The benchmark uses the same architecture, learning rate, data splits, and fairness definition for all algorithms, so the only variable is the loss formula itself.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a fairness trainer on a small census dataset (500 rows, binary fairness: high income / low income). Implement two loss functions: one that adds fairness penalty directly, one that uses Lagrange multiplier reweighting. Train both on the same data 10 times each (random seeds). Plot the fairness-accuracy tradeoff curve for each. Show that the Lagrange method produces a different curve — ideally one that's shifted higher (better fairness for same accuracy loss), because the Lagrange approach dynamically adjusts how strongly to push fairness, while the direct penalty uses a fixed weight that may be too weak or too strong.
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that the two algorithms take different paths through the fairness-accuracy space; one is not simply a rescaled version of the other, proving the benchmark can actually distinguish them.
